explain.say: In 1928 the scientist Alexander Fleming came back from holiday to his London laboratory and found something odd on a dish of bacteria he had left out. It led to one of the most important medicines ever.

explain.say: A mould spore had drifted onto the dish and grown into a fuzzy patch. It was Penicillium, a relative of the blue-green mould on old bread and oranges.

stages.ask: Why did the mould kill the bacteria?

stages.label: Mass production
stages.ask: How was penicillin made in large amounts?

explain.say: All around the mould was a clear ring where the bacteria had died. Fleming realised the mould was making a substance that killed bacteria, and he named it penicillin.

stages.label: Mass production
stages.ask: How was penicillin made in large amounts?

explain.say: Penicillin was very hard to purify. Around 1940, Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and Norman Heatley in Oxford extracted enough to test, and by 1944 factories were making it in huge amounts.

faq.q: Why did the mould kill the bacteria?
faq.a: Penicillium makes penicillin, which stops many bacteria building their cell walls, so they burst as they try to grow. In nature this may help the mould compete with bacteria for food.

faq.q: How was penicillin made in large amounts?
faq.a: Scientists grew the mould in huge tanks. In 1943 a mouldy melon from a market in Peoria, Illinois, gave a strain that made far more penicillin, and production soared during the Second World War.
asks: Where did the best penicillin mould come from?

faq.q: Who won the Nobel Prize for penicillin?
faq.a: Alexander Fleming, Howard Florey and Ernst Chain shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1945.
No. Penicillin and other antibiotics work only against bacteria. Colds and flu are caused by viruses, so antibiotics do not help them.

faq.q: Is the mould on bread the same as penicillin?
faq.a: No. Some bread moulds are related to Penicillium, but eating mouldy food will not treat an infection and can make you ill. Medicines are purified and made in carefully controlled factories.
asks: Can mouldy bread cure an infection?

facts: Alexander Fleming noticed penicillin's effect on bacteria in 1928 at St Mary's Hospital, London.
Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
In 1943 a mouldy cantaloupe melon in Peoria, Illinois, provided a Penicillium strain that made far more penicillin.
